challenges.headline: Build before checking existing circuits
challenges.premise: Manager approval with escalation is a new feature to build.
challenges.alternative: The platform already has absence management and approval circuits shared across modules. Switching on or configuring existing approval and delegation, and adding only what is missing, may cover most of the need.
challenges.consequence: Building a parallel escalation mechanism duplicates the shared circuit engine and risks inconsistent behaviour across the modules that use it.
challenges.recommendation: Audit what the current leave approval and any delegation feature already do, and size the build only on the gap.

challenges.headline: What 'manager is away' means
challenges.premise: The system can simply tell when the manager is away and reroute.
challenges.alternative: Routing at submission from the manager's declared leave or a delegate they set is synchronous and simple. A timeout-based re-route needs a timer, a visible pending state and protection against two people deciding. Starting with declared absence plus a reminder keeps the first release small.
challenges.consequence: Without a choice, the team may build both, or a timer that fires on a request the manager is about to decide, producing conflicting decisions.
challenges.recommendation: Decide with the client which trigger defines 'away' before design, and treat the other as a later increment.

challenges.headline: Approval as a single decision
challenges.premise: A manager's yes or no is enough to approve leave.
challenges.alternative: Approval on this platform typically implies a balance or quota check (paid leave, RTT) and possibly several levels depending on leave type or duration. Scoping the first release to the manager step plus the balance check makes that explicit.
challenges.consequence: Treating approval as a flag and discovering the balance check and extra levels late multiplies scope and touches French leave rules.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm whether the balance check and multi-level approval are in scope for this release.

page.title: Manager leave approval with escalation
page.recommendation: Decide first whether to build anything new. We recommend auditing the existing leave approval and delegation capabilities, then extending the shared approval circuit with a single, clearly defined escalation trigger, starting with the manager's declared absence and a fallback approver.
page.why: You asked for managers to approve leave with an escalation when the manager is away. The platform already has absence management and approval circuits shared across modules, so part of this may exist or be a configuration away. Pinning down what 'away' means keeps the first release small and avoids conflicting decisions.
page.cost_and_risk: The main effort is the escalation trigger and its fit with the shared approval circuit. The risk that matters most is that a change to that shared circuit affects other modules, or that two people decide the same request.

challenges.headline: Build before checking what exists
challenges.premise: Manager approval with escalation is a new feature to be built.
challenges.alternative: The platform already has absence management and approval circuits shared across modules. If they support single-level approval and delegation, the request may be met by configuration, or by a small extension of the existing circuit.
challenges.consequence: Building a parallel escalation mechanism would duplicate the shared circuit and risk diverging from the other modules that use it.
challenges.recommendation: Audit what the current circuit already does for leave, including delegation, before estimating anything.

challenges.headline: What 'away' actually means
challenges.premise: The system can tell when a manager is away and then escalate.
challenges.alternative: Two different triggers exist: a declared absence (approved leave or out-of-office) routes at submission, while a response timeout (no decision after N days) catches managers who are present but silent. A timeout needs no availability data and covers both cases, optionally with a declared-absence shortcut.
challenges.consequence: Escalating only on declared absence leaves silent managers stalling requests, and needs reliable absence data that may not exist. Escalating only on timeout delays requests the system already knew would stall.
challenges.recommendation: Decide with the client which trigger they mean, and start with the timeout, since it works without extra data.

challenges.headline: Approval without a balance check
challenges.premise: Approval is a manager's yes or no.
challenges.alternative: On this platform, leave approval usually carries a balance or quota check (paid leave, RTT) and sometimes a second approval level. Treating those as part of the design from the start avoids reworking the circuit later.
challenges.consequence: A circuit built as a plain yes/no that later needs balance validation and multiple levels is reworked once escalation is already layered on it.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm whether balance checks and multi-level approval are in scope for this release or explicitly deferred.

complexity_reasons: escalation logic inside a circuit shared across modules
possible per-client configuration of delay and target
requests already in flight at rollout
briefs.cost_driver: extending the shared approval circuit without affecting other modules
risks: A change to the shared approval circuit and permission rules may ripple into other modules and screens.
The original manager and the escalation recipient can both act on the same request, producing conflicting decisions unless one decision locks the request.
The escalation target may also be away, or may not exist (employee with no manager, manager requesting their own leave), leaving requests stuck.
Leave data is HR data under GDPR, and the temporary rights given to an escalation recipient widen who can see it.
Requests already pending at rollout need a defined treatment, or they stay on the old behaviour.

opportunities.text: Make escalation a reusable capability of the shared approval circuit, with a configurable trigger and target, rather than a leave-specific rule.
Offer per-client configuration of the escalation delay and target, since approval circuits are already client-specific on this platform.

next_steps: Audit the existing approval circuit and absence module to see what single-level approval and delegation already cover.
Hold a short session with the client to settle the escalation trigger (declared absence or timeout), the target and whether escalation ends in a defined fallback.
Confirm scope for balance checks and multi-level approval, and whether the rule is standard or per client.
Estimate and sequence the build once those answers are in, starting with the timeout-based escalation.

decisions.decision: Treat this as an extension of the existing absence module and shared approval circuit rather than a separate mechanism.

page.title: Manager approval with escalation: build or configure?
page.recommendation: Before committing to a build, decide whether the existing approval circuit can deliver this. We recommend a short audit of the current absence module and circuit, then extending that circuit with a timeout-based escalation to a defined fallback approver if it falls short.
page.why: You asked for manager approval with an escalation when the manager is away. Your platform already has absence management and approval circuits shared across modules, so part of this may already exist. Reusing the shared circuit avoids a parallel mechanism. A timeout trigger works whether the manager is absent or simply silent, and needs no availability data to be reliable.
page.cost_and_risk: The main cost is extending the shared approval circuit without disturbing the other modules that rely on it. The risk that matters most is two people deciding the same request, or an escalation that has nobody to land on, which leaves requests stuck. The treatment of requests already pending at rollout also needs deciding.

open.would_change: If control or compliance is the driver rather than speed, the history of who decided or escalated becomes a core requirement.

challenges.headline: Build before checking existing approvals
challenges.premise: A new escalation capability must be built for the leave approval step.
challenges.alternative: The platform already offers approval circuits, which are client-specific by design. Configuring an extra escalation level or delegation step in that circuit may cover most of the need without a new engine.
challenges.consequence: A parallel escalation mechanism would duplicate logic in a circuit shared across modules, and the two could diverge on permissions and notifications.
challenges.recommendation: Check what the current approval circuit and any delegation feature already do before estimating any build.

challenges.headline: What 'away' actually means
challenges.premise: The system can tell when a manager is away and escalate accordingly.
challenges.alternative: Escalating on a timeout after a set number of days needs no knowledge of the manager's status. A declared delegation or the manager's own approved leave is a cheaper, status-driven trigger. Combining the two gives a safety net.
challenges.consequence: A status-only trigger misses managers who are unreachable without having declared it. A timer-only trigger adds queued jobs, reminders and a window where the request sits in limbo.
challenges.recommendation: Agree one primary trigger and one fallback before design, and name a last-resort recipient so that no request can stall.

challenges.headline: Escalation hides a wider approval build
challenges.premise: Approval is a simple manager yes or no with an escalation branch.
challenges.alternative: Leave approval normally implies a balance check and possibly several levels. Scoping the first release to the manager step plus one escalation level, with the balance check confirmed explicitly, keeps the build bounded.
challenges.consequence: If balance checks and paid leave and RTT rules are discovered mid-build, the work grows well beyond an escalation feature.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm now whether the balance check is in scope and whether it differs by leave type.

page.title: Leave approval with escalation: reuse before building
page.recommendation: Decide whether this escalation should be built new or configured on the approval circuit the platform already has. We recommend checking that circuit first, then building only the missing piece: a manager approval step with one escalation level and a guaranteed last-resort approver.
page.why: You want requests not to stall when a manager is away. The approval circuit is shared across modules and is client-specific by design, so a separate escalation mechanism risks duplicating logic and diverging on permissions and notifications. The request does not yet say how the system should know a manager is away, or who catches the request next, and those two answers decide whether this is a simple status rule or a timer-driven process.
page.cost_and_risk: The main cost is the escalation trigger and its fit with the shared approval circuit. The risk that matters most is a change to that circuit affecting other modules, together with requests still stalling if the escalation target is also away.
